But she held the newspaper rolled like a scepter, his advertisement turned up to prove she was there solely at his bidding—and yet the gold band, the photographs ... a mother, then. **After Ivan Albright's *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida***

She arrived as near to virginal as girls came in those days—which is to say, young, her dewy cheeks flushed with the daring of her own arrival. He had hoped for something with more edge. Yet she held the newspaper rolled like a scepter, his advertisement turned outward as if to prove she'd come solely at his bidding—and still, the gold band, the photographs... a mother, then.

He settled her into the old garden chair, the same one he retreated to each evening, where the first tug of the cord sent the bulb swinging like the lamps in the medic's tent above the wounded—those swaddled shapes that moaned with each release of the Screaming Meemies, their calculated shrieks distant enough to mistake for crickets. All around him, the matted gauze and ether stirred an itch so fierce he could barely trace the clean curve of each opening incision.

I close my eyes and walk straight to it. Nothing remarkable, yet it remains—wicker fraying beneath my steadying fingers.

---

# Rewritten Text

Inspired by IVAN ALBRIGHT's *Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida*

She showed up about as innocent as young women got back then—meaning simply youthful, her fresh face reddening at her own boldness. He'd wanted someone with a bit more grit. Still, she clutched the newspaper twisted up like a royal staff, his ad displayed outward as evidence she'd come purely because he'd summoned her—yet that wedding ring, those pictures... clearly a mother. He settled her into the weathered garden chair, the very one he retreated to each night when the initial pull of the cord set the bulb swaying like those lamps hanging in the field hospital above the wounded, bandaged figures who cried out whenever the Screaming Meemies detonated, their calculated wails distant enough that he mistook them for crickets—all while the caked bandages and anesthetic around him stirred up an itch so fierce he could barely trace each smooth line where flesh parted.

I close my eyes and move directly toward it. There's nothing remarkable about it, yet it remains—the wicker unraveling beneath my steadying fingertips.

# Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida

The poem opens in the charged stillness of Ivan Albright's studio, where the painting takes its slow, deliberate shape. Into this space walks Ida—young, and yet Albright renders her with a strange, unsettling purity, a near-virginal quality that seems to defy what we know of her circumstances, of the era's harder truths about women who answer newspaper advertisements to sit for strange men in strange rooms. She arrives carrying the very proof of her legitimacy: a rolled newspaper clutched like a scepter, the advertisement itself becoming her credential, her explanation for being there at all. But other objects complicate this appearance of innocence—a gold band catching the light, photographs tucked away that she perhaps did not mean to reveal, small proofs that she is someone's mother, that a fuller life exists beyond the frame of this single sitting.

Albright seats her in an old wicker chair, worn and creaking, and it is this chair—more than the woman herself—that becomes the poem's true subject, the object that unlocks memory. For this is the same chair, or one so like it, that carries him back to evenings he has never fully left behind. Above them, a lightbulb swings on its cord, and in that small, mundane motion he finds himself transported: not to his studio at all, but to the flickering lamps of a medic's tent, years and continents away.

There, memory surfaces in fragments, sensory and unbidden. He remembers the wounded, their moans folding into the artillery's distant thunder—the men called it "Screaming Meemies," that terrible whistle and burst—though from where he crouched, sketching, the sounds seemed impossibly small, no louder than crickets singing in a summer field, as if distance could soften what proximity could not. He remembers, too, the itch of gauze against his own skin, the sharp chemical sting of ether in the air, and how he tried, even then, even there, to render clean anatomical lines—the curve of a shoulder, the arc of a wrist—as though beauty and order might be salvaged from chaos through the simple, stubborn act of drawing.

The poem's final movement pulls us back into the present tense, into the quiet aftermath of memory's flood. The speaker closes his eyes, and in that darkness he returns—not to war, not entirely, but to this room, this ordinary afternoon made suddenly significant by all it has summoned. His hand finds the wicker chair, its surface fraying now with age and use, and he touches it the way one touches a scar: for comfort, for confirmation that he is here, that he has survived into this softer, stranger present, where a woman named Ida waits patiently for him to finish seeing her.
outputs.L4:
# Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida

I arranged her in the wicker chair—
plain Ida, church-going, wedding-ringed,
her thick fingers curled around a compact,
the powder puff hovering like a small mercy
above the roadmap of her throat.

She didn't know the studio light was truth,
harsher than any confessor.
Every crease of her collapsing chin
was a country I had already mapped
in canvas tents outside Neufchâteau,
where boys' faces opened like books
nobody wanted to read twice.

I was twenty then, sketching for the medical corps,
learning the vocabulary of wounds—
the specific red that means artery,
the yellow-white of exposed bone,
the way a face becomes unrecognizable
to itself before it becomes unrecognizable to others.

Screaming meemies overhead all that autumn,
their whistle a soprano note before the world convulsed.
We flinched, then returned to our stretchers,
our basins, the business of holding men together
long enough for someone else to fail them.

Now Ida sits patient in her chair,
unaware I am giving her the same attention
I gave to the shattered jaws, the boys
who kept asking for their mothers
in languages none of the nurses spoke.

I paint her wattled neck, her spotted hands,
each vein a thin blue river of returning memory.
This is not cruelty. This is the only tenderness
I learned in tents that smelled of ether and rot—
to look, and look again, and refuse to look away,
to render even decay as a kind of reverence.

The wicker creaks. Ida shifts her weight,
modest in her house dress, unaware
that I am translating her mortality
into the same exacting brushstrokes
I once used to record what shrapnel does
to a body that still, somehow, keeps breathing.

Somewhere outside my studio, war goes on
being fought by other men in other trenches,
and I am still here, mixing my whites and grays,
still hearing that thin scream descending,
still waiting—canvas after canvas—
for the impact that will finally arrive,
that will let me set down my brush
and call the wound, at last, complete.
outputs.L5:
# After Ivan Albright

There is a particular kind of looking that Ivan Albright's paintings demand—a looking that lingers past comfort, past the polite glance we typically give to portraits and still lifes, into something closer to confrontation. To come after Albright, whether as a viewer decades later or as an artist working in his shadow, is to reckon with an unflinching vision of decay, mortality, and the flesh's slow betrayal.

Albright, the American painter known for his meticulous, almost obsessive rendering of aging and decomposition, built a career on paintings that refused the comfortable lies most art tells about beauty and time. His most famous work, "Picture of Dorian Gray," created for the 1945 film adaptation of Oscar Wilde's novel, distilled his entire philosophy into a single grotesque image: the corruption that vanity tries to hide, made visible in every sagging fold and diseased patch of skin. But this was not merely illustration—it was Albright's worldview compressed into paint, the culmination of a life spent staring at what most people look away from.

To work "after Albright" is to inherit a peculiar burden. His influence doesn't invite imitation so much as confrontation. Artists who take up his themes—the body's inevitable decline, the horror lurking beneath surfaces, the moral weight embedded in physical matter—must contend with his radical patience. Albright sometimes spent years on a single canvas, building up layers of paint until objects seemed to vibrate with an unbearable, hyper-real presence. This was not speed or spontaneity but a kind of devotional slowness, as though only obsessive attention could do justice to the horror and wonder of physical existence.

What remains, after Albright, is a challenge to easy aesthetics. He asked viewers to accept ugliness as a legitimate subject of serious art, to see in decay not merely an ending but a truth equal in weight to any beauty. After him, the corroded doorknob, the swollen knuckle, the yellowed tooth all became worthy of the same scrutiny once reserved for youth and symmetry. This is his lasting inheritance: an insistence that art's obligation is not to flatter reality but to see it, completely, without blinking.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ekphrastic poem inspired by Ivan Albright's painting "Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida," blending the sitter's story with the artist's wartime memories.
counterfactuals.output:
**Into the World There Came a Soul Called Ida**
*after Ivan Albright, 1929–30*

I.

He asked her to sit still an hour, then ten years.
She came young—Ida from the neighborhood,
paid to hold a mirror to her face
while powder settled like a first snow
that never fully falls, just hangs.

He painted what the light refused to hide.

II.

In France he'd knelt in canvas tents and drawn
the wounds before the surgeons closed them—
a jaw unhinged, a chest thrown open like a drawer,
the meat of men still breathing, still afraid.
He learned the exact green a wound turns
on its third unhealed day,
the yellow at the edge of bruised,
how flesh, when parted, tells the truth
no uniform can button over.

That was his other schooling: to look
until the looking became a kind of mercy—
not away, but *into*.

III.

So when Ida sat, plump-armed, half-undressed,
reaching for her rouge, her ribbon,
he gave her all of it—the war he carried home
in his wrist, in the brush's patient crawl.
Her skin became the field hospital's light:
not young, not old, but *timed*,
each crease a suture holding shape
against what wants to come undone.

The vanity table holds its little lies—
comb, puff, the oval glass—
but he painted through them
to the soul age wears like a coat
too heavy to take off.

IV.

Is this cruelty? He'd say no.
He'd say: I have seen what waits
under the smoothest face,
and I loved it enough to make it slow,
to make you stand before it
and not look away—

the way I couldn't,
the way none of us,
once we've seen, ever fully can.

V.

Ida is not dying in this painting.
She is only what we all are becoming,
caught in a single held breath
between the tent flap and the mirror,
between the boy he was
and the man who could not stop
seeing wounds
wherever there was skin.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a persona poem in the voice of Ivan Albright reflecting on painting Ida, weaving in memories of working as a medical illustrator during WWI.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ivan Albright, Speaking of Ida

I have always painted what the mirror
refuses to lie about—the way flesh
remembers everything it has survived.

Before Ida, there was Dijon, 1918,
the surgical tents where I learned my true trade:
sketching the body's honest catastrophes.
A boy's shoulder opened like a book
no one wanted to read twice.
I drew what the surgeons needed—
not beauty, but accuracy,
the particular blue of dying tissue,
the way muscle separates from bone
like an argument finally settled.

They taught me to look and keep looking
past the moment when looking becomes unbearable.
That the wound is also a kind of truth-telling.
That skin is only a temporary agreement
between the body and time.

So when Ida sat for me—
mirror in hand, powder puff, that blue robe
sliding from her shoulder like a confession—
I painted the war I never stopped fighting.
Every crease of her elbow, every vein
mapping its slow blue river toward the heart,
I gave her what the medical tents gave me:
the refusal to look away.

Critics said I made her monstrous.
They wanted Venus. I gave them Verdun.
I gave them what the young men's mothers
never got to see—the actual architecture
of a body keeping its appointment with decay.

Ida, forgive me. I did not paint you cruel.
I painted you *true*, the way I once traced
a soldier's ruined hand so the surgeons
could remember, could learn, could save
the next boy's fingers from the same undoing.

Your sagging breast, your thickened knuckles,
the powder failing on your papery cheek—
this is not an insult. This is elegy.
This is what I learned in France:
that decay deserves a witness,
that every collapsing thing
still wants, still deserves,
to be looked at with love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of poetic prose that merges art criticism, historical detail about Albright's war experience, and a sudden shift into first-person present-tense memory.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Looking at Ivan Albright's "That Which I Should Have Done I Did Not Do"

The paint does not sit on the canvas so much as it accumulates there, sediment upon sediment, like something the body has been forced to remember against its will. Albright worked this surface for a decade, layering pigment until the door itself seems to sweat, until the wreath of funeral flowers curdles into something closer to rot than commemoration. This is not decay rendered—this is decay's actual texture, its patience, its terrible thoroughness.

He learned this patience in France, in 1918, at the base hospitals where he drew for the medical corps. Not soldiers charging, not the clean mythology of sacrifice, but the aftermath: the wounds that refused to become scars, the flesh that had to be documented in its actual, ongoing catastrophe. He made over eight thousand illustrations of injury. Each one a small, exact refusal to look away. The Army wanted records; what Albright kept was the knowledge that the body is not a metaphor for anything. It simply insists.

This is why his surfaces never resolve. Why the green of that door is not one green but forty greens fighting each other beneath the same skin of varnish. He had seen what forty kinds of dying looked like on a single afternoon in a canvas tent, and no idea of beauty could survive that kind of witnessing intact.

*I am standing in my grandfather's hallway and I am eleven years old and the smell of his sickness has gotten into the wallpaper, has gotten into the doorframe, and I understand for the first time that a house can hold a body's failing the way a jar holds water, that some rooms do not air out, that I will remember this particular yellow light for the rest of my life whether I want to or not—*

The door in Albright's painting will never open. That was never its purpose. It exists to make visible the accumulation itself: what time does to matter, what memory does to time, how the past does not fade so much as thicken, layer on layer, until looking at it becomes its own kind of wound.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short literary work titled after Albright's painting that moves between third-person narrative about the sitter and a jarring first-person fragment at the end.
counterfactuals.output:
# Picture of Dorian Gray (After Albright)

The woman who sat for the portrait had not asked to be immortalized in decay. That was the artist's doing, his particular genius, the way he built color like sediment, like something accreted over centuries rather than painted in an afternoon. She sat in the good chair by the window, wore her blue dress, held her hands the way her mother had taught her—loose, unclenched, a lady's hands. She thought of nothing in particular. She thought of the marketing she would need to do that evening, the state of the icebox, whether her son had remembered his key.

The artist saw something else. He always did. Under his brush the light through the window turned sickly, the blue of her dress curdled toward green, and the flowers in the vase beside her—which had been fresh, which she had cut herself that morning—began to spot and brown as if the canvas itself were aging faster than the room around it. He worked for months. She sat for him perhaps a dozen times, then he continued without her, building the thing up in her absence, layering ochre and umber until her face in the painting bore only a family resemblance to the face that had once occupied the chair.

When it was finished he did not show her. This was not unusual; artists rarely did, and she had already been paid, already returned to her life, which continued in its ordinary way—the marketing, the icebox, the son who came home late and smelling of cigarettes he thought she couldn't detect. She grew older according to the normal schedule. Her hands began to spot. Her hair, which had been dark, went the color of ash and then the color of nothing at all. She did not think of the painting. She had nearly forgotten it existed, filed away in some collector's parlor or municipal archive, gathering its own particular dust.

It hung, eventually, in a museum. People stood before it and felt a specific unease they could not name, something in the register between disgust and recognition. They read the little placard. They moved on to the next room, the next arrangement of paint and intention, and did not think again about the woman in the blue dress, if she had existed, if she had sat in a real chair in a real light and thought about nothing in particular while something else was being made of her.

—

*I am the chair. I am the dress gone to rot before it ever left the loom. I am the flower that browned in the vase while she was still cutting it fresh that morning, still whole, still walking toward me with her scissors and her ordinary hands, not knowing I was already waiting on the other side of the paint, already old, already this.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an experimental poem about a painter's model that incorporates imagery of gauze, ether, and wartime field hospitals, ending with a sensory memory of an old garden chair.
counterfactuals.output:
**Studies in Gauze and Ether**

*i.*

Hold           still
the word arrives before the body does,
before the brush knows what stillness costs.

She learned it first in canvas tents,
the folding cots, the lamps turned low as breath—
*hold still* the surgeon said, and the gauze
came down like a curtain rehearsing its own weight.

*ii.*

Now the studio smells the same:
turpentine, thin and sweet,
a cousin to the ether
that once made the wounded boys
forget which limb was theirs.

She sits. The light falls clinical, north-facing,
honest as a scalpel.
The painter squints the way the surgeon did—
*measuring, measuring*—
before the first incision of red into white.

*iii.*

Muslin       draped across her shoulder,
             a bandage
                       loosened from its purpose,
becoming drapery, becoming
                       Grecian, becoming
                                    a wound made beautiful
                                                by not being one.

She thinks: *I have been dressed like this before.*
Not for beauty. For triage.
For the tagging of the almost-dead.

*iv.*

Brushstroke as suture.
Color bleeding at the edges
the way morphine bleeds a face
into something calmer than itself.

The painter says *don't move*
and she thinks of the boy
who couldn't anyway,
his chest rising once, a tide
going out and not returning,
gauze pulled up like a modest sheet
over a canvas already finished.

*v.*

*Hold still.*
The phrase again, worn smooth
as a coin passed hand to hand
through decades of the same demand—
soldier, model, sister, saint—
all of them practicing
the discipline of not flinching
while someone else decides
what the body means.

*vi.*

And then—unbidden, the way memory
refuses the order of things—

the garden chair.

Green paint gone to lichen at the joints,
wicker soft with thirty summers,
warm the way only wood left in sun is warm,
a heat that climbs into the palms like language.

She is eight. Barefoot. The grass
unbandaged, uninjured, only grass.
The chair creaks the specific creak
of things that have held weight before
and will again—

no gauze, no ether, no white coats
folding down like wings—

only the smell of cut lawn,
her grandmother's hand
brushing a moth from her hair,

and stillness, for once,
not a command
but a gift she didn't know
to call by that name yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
